blocks.text: 2. The Primary and Circumstantial Retributions of the Land of Ultimate Bliss

inline.s: [The primary and circumstantial retributions of the Land of Ultimate Bliss]The circumstantial retribution (the environs) and the primary retribution (the inhabitants) of the Land of Ultimate Bliss. [Primary retribution]The body and mind of sentient beings — this is the very substance of the karmic fruit attained in response to past karmic causes. [Circumstantial retribution]The karmic fruit upon which body and mind dwell, such as lands, the earth, houses, and implements — that is, the conditions of livelihood.

blocks.text: The Land Adorned and Purified, Chapter Eleven

inline.s: [The land adorned and purified]The land’s
adornment and purity.

[The Buddha told Ananda: that realm of Ultimate Bliss is endowed with immeasurable merit and virtue and fully adorned. Forever there is no name at all for any suffering, any of the eight difficulties, any evil realm, or any affliction by demons. Nor is there any difference of the four seasons, of cold and heat, or of rain and shade. Moreover there are none of the great and small rivers and seas, none of the hills, mounds, pits, and hollows, none of the thorns and gravel, and none of the iron-enclosing mountain, Mount Sumeru, or mountains of earth and stone. The ground alone is natural seven-jewel and gold, broad and level and straight, without bound or limit. Subtle, wondrous, strange and lovely, pure and adorned, it surpasses all the worlds of the ten directions.]

The Buddha told Ananda: the Land of Ultimate Bliss is endowed with immeasurable merit and virtue and fully adorned. Forever there is no name at all for any suffering, any of the difficulties (the eight difficulties), any evil realm (the three evil paths), or any affliction by demons (since there is not even a name for them, still less can such things arise). Nor is there any difference of the four seasons (spring, summer, autumn, winter), of cold and heat, or of rain and shade (rainy days and overcast days). Moreover there are none of the great and small rivers, lakes, and seas, none of the hills, mounds, pits, and hollows, none of the thorns and gravel, and none of the iron-enclosing mountain, Mount Sumeru, or mountains made of earth and stone. The ground is wholly natural seven-jewel and gold, broad and level and straight, without bound or limit. The Land of Ultimate Bliss is subtle, wondrous, strange and lovely, pure and adorned, surpassing all the worlds of the ten directions.

[Many sufferings]The various kinds of suffering. Classified, there are the three sufferings, the eight sufferings, the ten sufferings, and the hundred-and-ten sufferings. [Three sufferings]The suffering of suffering, the suffering of decay, and the suffering of conditioning. First, the suffering of suffering: human beings already have a body of birth and death, which is suffering enough; with the many sufferings pressing upon them, it is suffering piled on suffering, hence it is called the suffering of suffering. Second, the suffering of decay: a pleasurable state that appears at times, and the suffering felt once it is lost. Third, the suffering of conditioning: the suffering that all conditioned things are impermanent, flowing on unceasingly and never at rest. [Eight sufferings]First, the suffering of birth, the pain of being born; second, the suffering of old age, the pain of growing old and weak; third, the suffering of sickness, the pain of illness; fourth, the suffering of death, the pain at the moment of dying; fifth, the suffering of separation from the loved, the pain of parting from those one loves; sixth, the suffering of meeting the hated, the pain of being together with one’s enemies; seventh, the suffering of seeking in vain, the pain of what one seeks being unattained; eighth, the suffering of the blazing of the five aggregates, because the illusory, false body and mind and so on of the five aggregates (form, feeling, conception, conditioning, consciousness) give rise in the realm of the six objects to delusion and karma, and are subjected to torment, as if aflame, a suffering that cannot be stilled. [The ten sufferings and the hundred-and-ten sufferings]Concerning the ten and the hundred-and-ten sufferings, Master Lianchi’s Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra says:

“The ten sufferings: as the Bodhisattva-piṭaka Sūtra states: first, the suffering of birth; second, the suffering of old age, up to the tenth, the suffering of the round of birth and death. The hundred-and-ten sufferings: as the Yogācārabhūmi (Yoga Treatise) states: first, the suffering of the undifferentiated round; second, the suffering of desire; third, the suffering of delusion, up to the fifty-fifth suffering; then nine kinds of suffering, which from among the nine are in turn unfolded into fifty-five, and these combined make the hundred-and-ten sufferings.”

[Eight difficulties]The eight places and circumstances in which seeing and hearing the Dharma are obstructed, namely: the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, the Northern Kuru continent, the heaven of no-thought, the blind, deaf, and dumb, worldly intelligence and eloquent argument, and the time before the Buddha’s advent or after his passing. Among these, the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals belong to the three evil paths; because their karmic hindrance is too heavy, it is very hard for them to see and hear the Dharma. The people of the Northern Kuru continent have great good fortune, but do not know the Dharma, so they cannot put an end to birth and death. The heaven of no-thought is where non-Buddhist ascetics are born; the people there likewise cannot put an end to birth and death. Those afflicted with blindness, deafness, and dumbness naturally cannot see or hear the Dharma. Worldly intelligence and eloquent argument: worldly people who, relying on their petty cleverness, are unwilling to practice humbly, and may even slander the Dharma. To be born before the Buddha’s advent or after the Buddha’s nirvāṇa, one can see no Buddha and hear no Dharma.

[Affliction by demons (the four demons)]The harassment of the demons (the four demons). [Four demons]The demon of afflictions, the demon of the five aggregates, the demon of death, and the heavenly demon. The demon of afflictions refers to such habitual tendencies as greed, hatred, and delusion, which can harass body and mind. The demon of the five aggregates refers to the five aggregates of form, feeling, conception, conditioning, and consciousness, which can give rise to all suffering. The demon of death refers to death, which can cut off a person’s life-root of existence. The heavenly demon refers to the heavenly demon and non-Buddhist teachers who can ruin a person’s good deeds. [Mount Sumeru]Rendered in Chinese as the Wonderful High Mountain, the center of a small world. This mountain is formed of the four treasures of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal; no other mountain can match its height, so it is the king of mountains. [Iron-enclosing mountain]The iron mountain that encircles the salt sea and marks off a small world. [Seven treasures]Gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, amber, fine jade, and agate.
[Ananda, having heard this, addressed the World-honored One: if that land has no Mount Sumeru, then on what do the heaven of the Four Great Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa heaven rely to dwell?]

Ananda, hearing this, respectfully asked the World-honored One: if the Land of Ultimate Bliss has no Mount Sumeru, then on what do the heaven of the Four Great Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa heaven rely to dwell?

[On what do they rely to dwell]In ordinary Buddha-lands, the heaven of the Four Great Kings is on the flank of Mount Sumeru and the Trāyastriṃśa heaven on its summit; both rely on the mountain to dwell. Ananda, hearing the Buddha say that the Land of Ultimate Bliss has no Mount Sumeru, therefore asked this question.
[The Buddha told Ananda: the Yāma, the Tuṣita, and even all the heavens of the realm of form and the realm of formlessness — on what do they rely to dwell?]

The Buddha asked in return: the Yāma heaven, the Tuṣita heaven, even all these heavens of the realm of form and of the realm of formlessness — they are not on Mount Sumeru, so on what do they rely to dwell?

[All the heavens, on what do they rely to dwell]The heaven of the Four Great Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa heaven rely on Mount Sumeru to dwell, and are called the earth-dwelling heavens; all the heavens above the Yāma heaven dwell in the sky, and are called the sky-dwelling heavens.
[Ananda replied: it is by the force of inconceivable karma.]
Ananda respectfully replied: they dwell in the sky; this is caused by the force of inconceivable karma.
[Inconceivable]What cannot be reached by the thought or speech of sentient beings.

[The Buddha told Ananda: the inconceivable karma — can you know it? Your own body’s karmic fruit is inconceivable; the karmic retribution of sentient beings is likewise inconceivable; the wholesome roots of sentient beings are inconceivable; the holy power of the Buddhas and the worlds of the Buddhas are also inconceivable. The beings of that land, by the strength of their merit and virtue, dwell in the ground of the Buddha’s practice and conduct, and so, together with the Buddha’s transcendent power, this is how it can be so.]

The Buddha told Ananda: the inconceivable karma — can you know it? Your own retribution is inconceivable; the karmic retribution of sentient beings is likewise inconceivable; the wholesome roots of sentient beings are inconceivable; the holy power of the Buddhas (the power of the Buddhas) and the worlds of the Buddhas are also inconceivable. Because the beings of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, by the strength of their merit and virtue, dwell in the ground of Amitābha Buddha’s practice and conduct, and through Amitābha Buddha’s transcendent power, therefore the heaven of the Four Great Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa heaven of that land can dwell in reliance on the sky.
[Ground of practice and conduct]The ground of the accomplishment of Amitābha Buddha’s great vows, great practice, and great work.

[Ananda replied: the karmic cause and karmic fruit are inconceivable! In this matter I am in truth without any doubt. But for the sake of future beings, to break apart the net of doubt, I have asked this question.]

Ananda said to the Buddha: the karmic cause and karmic fruit are inconceivable! As for the heaven of the Four Great Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa heaven of the Land of Ultimate Bliss being able to dwell in reliance on the sky, I in truth have no doubt at all. It is only to break apart the doubts of future beings (because future beings may raise this question) that I have asked it.

[The Buddha told Ananda: the majestic, spiritual light of Amitābha Buddha is the most honored and supreme of all; the Buddhas of the ten directions cannot equal it. It universally shines upon the Buddha-lands of the East as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and likewise upon the South, West, and North, the four quarters, above, and below. As for the halo of light upon the crown of the head, it extends now one, two, three, or four yojanas, now a hundred, a thousand, a million, or a koṭi of yojanas. The light of other Buddhas shines now upon one or two Buddha-lands, now upon a hundred or a thousand Buddha-lands. Only Amitābha Buddha’s light universally shines upon immeasurable, boundless, countless Buddha-lands.]

The Buddha told Ananda: the majestic, spiritual light of Amitābha Buddha is most honored and supreme. The Buddhas of the ten directions cannot equal it. The halo upon his crown universally shines upon the Buddha-lands of the East as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and upon the South, West, and North, also as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, as well as the four quarters (southeast, southwest, northwest, northeast), above, and below, likewise as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. The halo of other Buddhas shines now upon one, two, three, or four yojanas, now upon a hundred, a thousand, ten-thousand, or a hundred-million yojanas; now upon one or two Buddha-lands, now upon a hundred or a thousand Buddha-lands. Only Amitābha Buddha’s light universally shines upon immeasurable, boundless, countless Buddha-lands.
[Halo upon the crown of the head]Buddhas and bodhisattvas have a body-light and a crown-light; “the halo upon the crown of the head” refers to the crown-light
the halo of light above the crown of the head). The Sūtra of the Amitābha Buddha (Wu translation) says:

“The light of Amitābha Buddha is the most honored, the first beyond compare. The light of all the Buddhas cannot equal it. Among the countless Buddhas of the eight directions, above and below, some Buddhas have a light in the crown of the head that shines seven fathoms; some have a light that shines one li; some two li; some five li; some ten li.
Some Buddhas have a light that shines six million li; some a light that shines over one Buddha-land; some two Buddha-lands; some four; some eight; some fifteen Buddha-lands.
Some Buddhas have a light that shines over two hundred thousand Buddha-lands.”
It also says:
“The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Ajita: the light in the crown of Amitābha Buddha’s head is exceedingly great light.”
yojana
A unit for measuring distance in India. It has three sizes, great, medium, and small: the great yojana is about eighty li; the medium yojana about sixty li; the small yojana about forty li.

[The near and far to which the light of the Buddhas shines is based upon the vows of their previous lives in seeking the Way and the size of their merit, which differ for each. When they became Buddhas, each received it accordingly. It is spontaneously achieved, not something prearranged.]

The near and far to which the light of the Buddhas shines is based on the fundamental vows of their previous lives in seeking the Way and the size of their merit, which differ for each. When they became Buddhas, each received it accordingly. This is the natural accomplishment of vow, practice, and karma; it is not something to be prearranged.

[The light of Amitābha Buddha is excellent and good, surpassing the brightness of the sun and moon by a thousand koṭis of times; he is the most honored among lights, the king among Buddhas. Therefore Amitābha Buddha is also named the Buddha of Immeasurable Light, the Buddha of Boundless Light, the Buddha of Unobstructed Light, the Buddha of Incomparable Light; he is also named the Light of Wisdom, the Light of Constant Illumination, the Light of Purity, the Light of Joy, the Light of Liberation, the Light of Peace, the Light Surpassing Sun and Moon, and the Light of Inconceivability.]

The light of Amitābha Buddha is exceedingly excellent and good, surpassing the brightness of the sun and moon by a thousand koṭis of times; he is the most honored among lights, the king among Buddhas. Therefore Amitābha Buddha (the Buddha of Immeasurable Life) is also named the Buddha of Immeasurable Light, the Buddha of Boundless Light, the Buddha of Unobstructed Light, the Buddha of Incomparable Light; he is also named the Light of Wisdom, the Light of Constant Illumination, the Light of Purity, the Light of Joy, the Light of Liberation, the Light of Peace, the Light Surpassing Sun and Moon, and the Light of Inconceivability.
[The most honored among lights, the king among Buddhas]The Sūtra of the Amitābha Buddha (Wu translation) says:
“The light of Amitābha Buddha is lovely and good, surpassing the brightness of the sun and moon by a hundred, a thousand, a koṭi, a hundred-million times.
He is the king among the Buddhas, the most honored among lights.”

[Amitābha Buddha (the Buddha of Immeasurable Life)]The Buddha of Immeasurable Life is Amitābha Buddha. Amitābha is a transliteration of the Sanskrit, while Immeasurable Life is a rendering of its meaning (amitāyus).

[Such a light universally shines upon all the worlds of the ten directions. Whatever beings encounter this light, their defilements are extinguished and goodness arises; their body and mind become gentle. If they are in the three evil paths, in places of extreme suffering, on seeing this light they all gain rest, and at the end of life they all attain liberation. If beings hear of the majestic, spiritual merit of this light and praise it day and night, with single heart without ceasing, then according to the wishes of their mind they will be born in that land.]
Such a

light universally shines upon all the worlds of the ten directions. Whatever beings encounter this light, their evil defilements are extinguished and wholesome roots arise; their body (conduct) and mind (intent) become gentle. If they are in the three evil paths, in places of extreme suffering, on seeing this light the torment and burning of their suffering all cease, and at the end of life they all attain liberation. If beings hear of the majestic, spiritual merit of this light and praise it day and night, with single heart without ceasing, then according to the wishes of their mind they will be born in that land (the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss).

blocks.text: Immeasurable Lifespan and Beings, Chapter Thirteen

inline.s: [Immeasurable lifespan and beings]The beings of the Land of Ultimate Bliss have an immeasurable lifespan, and their number is also immeasurable.

[The Buddha told Ananda: the lifespan of Amitābha Buddha is long and enduring, beyond reckoning or calculation. There is also a countless host of śrāvakas, whose spiritual wisdom is penetrating and clear, whose majestic power is freely attained, and who can hold all the worlds in the palm of their hand.]
